::: {.pageinfo}
Builds on [post 1](../what-you-hear/index.qmd). Uses derivatives, integrals and a little linear algebra; proofs and fine print are in folds you can skip. About 20 minutes. Written in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.
:::

A plucked or struck instrument's frequencies come from the spectrum of an [operator](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#operator), the numbers $\lambda_n$ for which $AX_n = \lambda_nX_n$: $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi$. For a plucked string the operator is a second derivative, and these frequencies are exactly in the ratios $1 : 2 : 3 : \cdots$.

## The string's operator {#operator}

The ideal string is perfectly flexible and uniform, held at both ends, with small motion and no losses: a plucked guitar or violin string. Let $u(x, t)$ be its height at the point $x$, $0 \le x \le L$, at time $t$, with tension $T$ and mass $\mu$ per unit length. Newton's law on each piece ([below](#newton)) gives $\mu u_{tt} = T u_{xx}$, where subscripts are [partial derivatives](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#partial-derivative). That is $u_{tt} = -Au$ with
$$
A = -\frac{T}{\mu}\,\frac{d^2}{dx^2} ,
$$
acting on functions on $[0, L]$ that are zero at both ends; we write $c = \sqrt{T/\mu}$. The tied ends are part of the operator: they fix its domain.

Its [eigenfunctions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#eigenfunction) are the sines:
$$
A\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L} = \lambda_n\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}, \qquad \lambda_n = \frac{T}{\mu}\Big(\frac{n\pi}{L}\Big)^2, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
$$
Mode $n$, released from rest, swings as $\cos(\sqrt{\lambda_n}\,t)$, so
$$
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = n \cdot \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} .
$$
The $1 : 2 : 3$ is $\sqrt{\lambda_n} \propto n$: two derivatives bring down $(n\pi/L)^2$, and the square root returns $n$. The same formula says that shorter, tighter or lighter strings sound higher: Mersenne's laws of 1636.[^mer]

A pluck starts many modes at once, and the string moves as their sum:

```{=html}

<div class="panel">

```

A piano wire adds bending stiffness:
$$
A = -\frac{T}{\mu}\,\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{EI}{\mu}\,\frac{d^4}{dx^4} ,
$$
where $E$ is steel's [Young's modulus](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#youngs-modulus) and $I$ the [second moment of area](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#second-moment) of the wire's cross-section, with $u = u_{xx} = 0$ at both ends. The eigenfunctions are the same sines; $\lambda_n$ gains a term $(EI/\mu)(n\pi/L)^4$, and the ratios become $1 : 2.001 : 3.005$ for a middle C wire ([the piano page](../other-instruments-same-recipe/piano.qmd#numbers)).

Here $\partial_x^2 = d^2/dx^2$; $c_0$ is the speed of sound; $\rho S$ is a bar's mass per unit length; $\sigma$ is the skin's mass per unit area, $T$ its tension per unit length, and $\Delta$ the [Laplacian](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#laplacian), in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$; $J_m$ is a [Bessel function](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#bessel) and $j_{mk}$ its $k$-th zero. The tine's shapes are $X_n = \cosh\beta_nx - \cos\beta_nx - \gamma_n(\sinh\beta_nx - \sin\beta_nx)$, with $\cos\beta_nL\cosh\beta_nL = -1$ and $\gamma_n = (\cosh\beta_nL + \cos\beta_nL)/(\sinh\beta_nL + \sin\beta_nL)$. The drum's shapes are drawn from above, coloured by sign.[^frtab]

A blown note is different: it sounds every whole-number multiple of its playing frequency, and the tube's resonances pick which partials are strong ([post 4](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#two-kinds)).

Whole-number ratios need $\sqrt{\lambda_n}$ proportional to whole numbers. A second derivative on an interval gives equally spaced [wavenumbers](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#wavenumber) $k_n$ ($n\pi/L$ for the string) and $\sqrt{\lambda_n} = ck_n$ (with $c_0$ for a tube), so the ratios are $1 : 2 : 3$, or $1 : 3 : 5$ with one closed end. The piano wire's added $k_n^4$ term pushes its partials slightly sharp. The tine's fourth derivative with a clamped and a free end has $\sqrt{\lambda_n} \propto \beta_n^2$, where the $\beta_nL$ are the unevenly spaced roots $1.875, 4.694, 7.855, \dots$ of $\cos\beta L\cosh\beta L = -1$. The disc's frequencies are proportional to the Bessel zeros $j_{mk}$, which are not equally spaced either.

[]{#hear}[]{#sound}[]{#force}[]{#chain}How the string's motion reaches your ear, through the bridge and the soundboard, is [post 2](../from-instrument-to-ear/index.qmd#sound)'s subject: the force on the bridge passes on every frequency $f_n$, and the soundboard and the room only rescale and delay each one.

## Where the equation comes from {#newton}

[]{#string}[]{#problem}Newton's law on a short piece of string gives the equation; with the tied ends, the plucked start $u(x, 0) = u_0(x)$ and the release at rest, $u_t(x, 0) = 0$, it pins down the motion.[^fr]

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 48 420 104" role="img" aria-label="A short piece of string between x and x plus dx on a hump; the tension pulls along the string at each end, and both pulls tilt downward, so the net force pulls the hump back down">
  <path class="dash" d="M 60 110 Q 210 30 360 100"/>
  <path class="acc" d="M 120 84 Q 210 54 300 78"/>
  <circle cx="120" cy="84" r="4" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="300" cy="78" r="4" class="fillacc"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 120 84 L 66 102"/><path class="neg" d="M 75.9 103.2 L 66 102 L 73.3 95.1"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 300 78 L 356 93"/><path class="neg" d="M 348.3 86.6 L 356 93 L 346.2 94.8"/>
  <text x="44" y="122">T</text><text x="364" y="110">T</text>
  <text x="112" y="70">x</text><text x="282" y="64">x + dx</text>
  <text x="104" y="142">upward part of each pull ≈ T × slope</text>
</svg>
```

The piece from $x$ to $x + dx$ is pulled along the string at each end with force $T$, and for a small slope the upward part of that pull is $T$ times the slope $u_x$. So the net upward force is $T u_x(x + dx) - T u_x(x) \approx T u_{xx}\,dx$, and it equals mass times acceleration, $\mu\,dx\,u_{tt}$:
$$
u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx} ,
$$
with $c = \sqrt{T/\mu}$ as above, the speed at which a ripple runs along the string. On a hump $u_{xx} < 0$, so the hump is pulled down. The model assumes a perfectly flexible string, small slopes and no friction (friction comes back [below](#fading)).

## The whole idea with two beads {#two-beads}

**Measured along the shapes $X_n$, the string's equation falls apart into separate springs, one per shape, and these are the only shapes that do this.** With two beads in place of the string, the whole idea fits in a $2 \times 2$ matrix.

Put two beads on a weightless string, at a third and two thirds of the way along, each carrying a third of the string's mass, $m = \mu L/3$. Call their heights $u_1$ and $u_2$. Each bead is pulled toward its neighbours, the tied ends counting as neighbours at height zero, so with spacing $\ell = L/3$,
$$
\begin{gathered}
\begin{pmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{pmatrix}'' = -K \begin{pmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{pmatrix},\\
K = \frac{T}{m\ell}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} .
\end{gathered}
$$
Each bead's acceleration depends on the other's height: the motion is *coupled*.

Now measure along two other directions: both beads together, $q_1 = (u_1 + u_2)/\sqrt2$, and the beads opposite, $q_2 = (u_1 - u_2)/\sqrt2$. Adding and subtracting the two equations gives
$$
q_1'' = -\frac{T}{m\ell}\,q_1, \qquad q_2'' = -\frac{3T}{m\ell}\,q_2 .
$$
Two separate springs, with frequencies in the ratio $1 : \sqrt3$; every motion of the beads is the two swings added.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="r2wrap" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1.6fr) minmax(0,1fr);gap:0.75rem;align-items:center">
    <canvas id="bdCanvas" style="height:170px" aria-label="Two beads on a string tied at both ends, moving"></canvas>
    <canvas id="bdPlane" style="height:170px" aria-label="The plane of the two heights u1 and u2, with the tilted q1 and q2 directions and the path of the motion"></canvas>
  </div>
  <div class="controls" role="group" aria-label="Start the two beads">
    <button type="button" id="bdS" aria-pressed="false">Together: q₁ only</button>
    <button type="button" id="bdD" aria-pressed="false">Opposite: q₂ only</button>
    <button type="button" id="bdM" aria-pressed="true">A mix</button>
    <button type="button" id="bdPlay" class="primary">Hear this motion</button>
  </div>
  <p class="cap">Slowed down. Right: the plane of the two heights, u₁ across and u₂ up. A mix traces a tangle; started along q₁ or q₂ alone, the motion runs straight along that tilted line. The sound puts the q₁ swing at 196 Hz.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

These directions work because $K$ only stretches them: $K(1, 1) = \frac{T}{m\ell}(1, 1)$ and $K(1, -1) = \frac{3T}{m\ell}(1, -1)$. They are the [eigenvectors](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#eigenvector) of $K$, and the stretch factors, its [eigenvalues](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#eigenvalue), are the springs' stiffnesses. They are also the string's first two shapes, one arch and two arches, sampled at the beads; the string is the same calculation with infinitely many beads.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>More beads, and the limit <span class="needs">matrices and limits</span></summary>

With $N$ beads, spacing $\ell = L/(N+1)$ and $m = \mu\ell$, the matrix is $K = \frac{T}{m\ell}\,\mathrm{tridiag}(-1, 2, -1)$. Its eigenvectors are the sines $\sin(n\pi x/L)$ sampled at the beads, with eigenvalues $\frac{c^2}{\ell^2}\,4\sin^2\frac{n\pi\ell}{2L}$, which tend to the string's $(n\pi c/L)^2$ as $N \to \infty$. (The frequency *ratios* tend to $1 : 2 : 3$ whatever the beads weigh; the frequencies themselves need $m = \mu\ell$.) Each row of the bead equation tends to $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$, by Taylor's theorem.

</details>
:::

## The string: the same move {#decoupling}

Here is why the [operator above](#operator) has the sines as its eigenfunctions, and why they turn the string into separate springs. For the string, the column of two heights becomes the whole curve $u(\cdot, t)$, and the matrix $K$ becomes $A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2$ on shapes zero at both ends.

**The shapes that $A$ only stretches.** Solve $AX = \lambda X$, that is $X'' = -k^2X$ with $k^2 = \lambda/c^2$ and $X(0) = X(L) = 0$. The solutions are $C_1\cos kx + C_2\sin kx$; the end $x = 0$ kills the cosine, and the end $x = L$ needs $\sin kL = 0$, so $kL = n\pi$. These are the sines $X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n = c^2(n\pi/L)^2$ of the first section; shape $n$ has $n$ arches. (No $\lambda \le 0$ works; the first fold below shows why.)

**Coordinates along them.** Measure the string by how much of each shape it contains, $q_n(t) = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L u(x, t)\,X_n(x)\,dx$, the continuous version of $q_1 = (u_1 + u_2)/\sqrt2$. Then each coordinate is a spring:
$$
\begin{aligned}
q_n'' &= \tfrac{2}{L}\!\int_0^L u_{tt}X_n = \tfrac{2}{L}\!\int_0^L c^2u_{xx}X_n\\
&= \tfrac{2}{L}\!\int_0^L c^2u\,X_n'' = -\lambda_n\,q_n .
\end{aligned}
$$
The middle step integrates by parts twice, moving both derivatives onto $X_n$; the boundary terms vanish because $u$ and $X_n$ are zero at the ends. (A pluck's corner has no $u_{xx}$; the second fold below handles it.) The last step is $X_n'' = -(\lambda_n/c^2)X_n$. So spring $n$ swings at $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi$, the frequency of [the first section](#operator).

**Why only these shapes.** Take any other family of perpendicular shapes $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$ that vanish at the ends and build every shape (an [orthonormal basis](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#orthonormal)), with coordinates $q_i = \int u\,\psi_i$. The same calculation gives $q_i'' = -\sum_j M_{ij}\,q_j$ with $M_{ij} = \int (A\psi_j)\psi_i$: each coordinate feels the others, as $u_1$ and $u_2$ did. The coordinates come apart exactly when $M$ is diagonal, which happens exactly when every $\psi_j$ is an eigenfunction. Nothing about the form of the solution was assumed.

**Why these shapes are enough.** Every starting shape is a sum of sines, $u_0 = \sum a_n X_n$: the Fourier sine series, the one theorem this post quotes rather than proves.[^ss]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>Decoupling happens exactly in an eigenbasis <span class="needs">inner products, orthonormal bases</span></summary>

Write $\langle u, w\rangle = \int_0^L u\,w\,dx$. (The main text's sines are orthogonal but have $\int X_n^2 = L/2$; normalised, $\sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(n\pi x/L)$, the factor $2/L$ in $q_n$ disappears.) For shapes $u, w$ vanishing at the ends, two integrations by parts give $\langle Au, w\rangle = c^2\!\int u'w' = \langle u, Aw\rangle$: $A$ is symmetric, like $K$. With $w = u$, $\langle Au, u\rangle = c^2\!\int (u')^2 > 0$ unless $u'$ is identically zero, which with $u(0) = 0$ forces $u = 0$; so $A$ is positive, and $AX = \lambda X$ forces $\lambda > 0$. That is why no $\lambda \le 0$ appears above.

**Proposition.** Let $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$ be an orthonormal basis of square-integrable shapes, each twice differentiable and zero at the ends, and let $q_j = \langle u, \psi_j\rangle$. Then $q_i'' = -\sum_j M_{ij}q_j$ with $M_{ij} = \langle A\psi_j, \psi_i\rangle$, and $M$ is diagonal if and only if every $\psi_j$ is an eigenfunction of $A$.

*Proof.* For a smooth solution, $q_i'' = \langle u_{tt}, \psi_i\rangle = -\langle Au, \psi_i\rangle = -\langle u, A\psi_i\rangle$, by symmetry of $A$; for a pluck, $q_i'' = -\langle u, A\psi_i\rangle$ is the definition of solution in the next fold, with $\varphi = \psi_i$. Expanding $u = \sum_j q_j\psi_j$ gives $q_i'' = -\sum_j q_j\langle\psi_j, A\psi_i\rangle = -\sum_j M_{ij}q_j$. If $A\psi_j = \kappa_j\psi_j$ for every $j$, then $M_{ij} = \kappa_j\langle\psi_j, \psi_i\rangle$ is diagonal. Conversely, $A\psi_j = \sum_i M_{ij}\psi_i$ (expansion in the basis), which is $M_{jj}\psi_j$ when $M$ is diagonal. $\square$

In a basis of polynomials vanishing at the ends (Gram–Schmidt on $x(L - x)x^k$), $M$ has nonzero entries far from the diagonal; with $L = 1$ its top-left entry is $10c^2$, just above $\lambda_1 = \pi^2c^2 \approx 9.87c^2$.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>What "solution" means for a pluck, and why there is exactly one <span class="needs">integration by parts, Cauchy–Schwarz</span></summary>

The triangle has a corner, where $u_{xx}$ does not exist, so the equation cannot hold there literally. The calculation of $q_n''$ above never needed $u_{xx}$ once the derivatives were moved onto $X_n$, which suggests the definition. *A solution* is a shape $u(t)$ with $\int u^2 < \infty$, changing continuously in mean square, such that for every smooth $\varphi$ vanishing at the ends, $\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\langle u, \varphi\rangle = -\langle u, A\varphi\rangle$, with $\langle u(0), \varphi\rangle = \langle u_0, \varphi\rangle$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\langle u, \varphi\rangle(0) = \langle v_0, \varphi\rangle$, where $v_0$ is the starting velocity (zero for a pluck). Smooth solutions satisfy it (integrate by parts); testing against all such $\varphi$ loses nothing, because they are dense in mean square. (L. C. Evans, [*Partial Differential Equations*](https://bookstore.ams.org/GSM/19.R), 2nd ed., AMS, 2010, section 7.2)

*Uniqueness.* With $\varphi = X_n$, each $q_n$ solves $q_n'' = -\lambda_nq_n$ with given $q_n(0), q_n'(0)$. That has exactly one solution: the difference $r$ of two has $r(0) = r'(0) = 0$, and $E = (r')^2 + \lambda_nr^2$ has $E' = 0$, so $r = 0$. Two solutions with the same start therefore have the same coordinates, so they are equal (the sines are a basis).

*Existence.* The series $\sum_n (a_n\cos\omega_nt + b_n\sin\omega_nt)X_n$, with $\omega_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$, $a_n = \frac{2}{L}\int u_0X_n$ and $b_n = \frac{2}{L}\int v_0X_n/\omega_n$, is a solution when the start has finite energy, $\int(u_0')^2 < \infty$ and $\int v_0^2 < \infty$. Integration by parts and Bessel's inequality give $\sum n^2a_n^2 < \infty$, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\sum |a_n| + |b_n| < \infty$; the series and its term-by-term time derivatives against $\varphi$ then converge uniformly, and the defining identity holds.

*Counting.* A mass on a spring has one eigenvalue and a two-dimensional space of motions ($\cos$ and $\sin$); two beads have two eigenvalues and four; the string has two dimensions of motion for each eigenvalue.

</details>
:::

## The pluck {#the-solution}

Each spring starts where the pluck puts it, at rest, so $q_n(t) = a_n\cos(2\pi f_n t)$ and
$$
\begin{gathered}
u(x, t) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} a_n \cos(2\pi f_n t)\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L},\\
a_n = \frac{2u_0(x_0)\,L^2\,\sin(n\pi x_0/L)}{\pi^2 n^2\,x_0(L - x_0)} ,
\end{gathered}
$$
for a triangle with its apex above $x_0$, at height $u_0(x_0)$. This is the motion in the demo at the top.

$a_n = 0$ when $nx_0/L$ is a whole number: a shape with a still point exactly where you pluck is never started. Pluck a fifth of the way along and the 5th, 10th, 15th, … shapes are missing.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The coefficients, and the exact motion <span class="needs">integration by parts</span></summary>

$a_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L u_0 X_n$. The triangle is straight on both sides of $x_0$, where its slope jumps by $-u_0(x_0)L/(x_0(L - x_0))$; integrating by parts twice turns $\int_0^L u_0X_n$ into minus that jump times $X_n(x_0)\,(L/n\pi)^2$, which gives the formula above.

The dashed curve in the demo is the exact motion in d'Alembert's form: extend $u_0$ to an odd function $\tilde u_0$ of period $2L$; then $u(x, t) = \frac12\big(\tilde u_0(x - ct) + \tilde u_0(x + ct)\big)$, two copies of the triangle running in opposite directions and flipping over at the ends. (J. le Rond d'Alembert, ["Recherches sur la courbe que forme une corde tenduë mise en vibration"](https://webusers.imj-prg.fr/%7Edavid.aubin/cours/Textes/Dalembert-HAB-1747-cordes-vibrantes.pdf), *Histoire de l'Académie royale des sciences et belles-lettres de Berlin* 3, 1747, published 1749, 214–219) Its sine series is the series above, since $\frac12[\sin(\theta - \phi) + \sin(\theta + \phi)] = \sin\theta\cos\phi$. The corners travel, which is why a solution has to be defined without $u_{xx}$.

</details>
:::

## Fading, and the light touch {#fading}

Real strings fade, high partials first, which is why a guitar note turns mellower as it rings.[^wolfe] Friction that acts the same way all along the string, like air drag, keeps the springs separate: each coordinate becomes a damped spring, $q_n'' + \gamma q_n' + \lambda_n q_n = 0$ with friction rate $\gamma$. So do losses that grow with frequency, as in Chaigne and Askenfelt's model of a piano string.[^ca]

Friction at one point is different, and it explains a trick every string player knows: rest a finger lightly at the middle of the string and the note jumps up an octave.[^wolfe2] The finger drains every shape that moves under it and cannot touch the shapes with a still point there. At the middle those are the even shapes, at $2f_1, 4f_1, 6f_1, \dots$, all multiples of $2f_1$: the octave. No frequency moved; the finger only chose which shapes keep ringing. String players call these [harmonics](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#string-harmonics); try them in the demo below.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <canvas id="tcCanvas" style="height:170px" aria-label="A string, the point where it is plucked, and a finger touching it lightly"></canvas>
  <div class="slider"><label for="tcX">Pluck point x₀</label><input type="range" id="tcX" min="0.04" max="0.5" step="0.01" value="0.2"><output id="tcXo">0.20 L</output></div>
  <div class="controls" role="group" aria-label="Where the finger touches">
    <span class="cap" style="margin-right:0.25rem">Touch lightly at</span>
    <button type="button" data-touch="0" aria-pressed="true">no touch</button><button type="button" data-touch="0.5">1/2</button><button type="button" data-touch="0.3333333">1/3</button><button type="button" data-touch="0.25">1/4</button><button type="button" data-touch="0.2">1/5</button>
  </div>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" id="tcPluck" class="primary">Pluck</button></div>
  <svg class="spec" id="tcSpec" viewBox="0 0 320 96" style="max-width:520px" aria-label="The size of each partial in the force on the bridge, a quarter second after the pluck"></svg>
  <div class="readout" id="tcRead"></div>
  <p class="cap">Move the pluck point to change the brightness; then touch the string lightly and pluck again. Stems: each partial of the force on the bridge 0.25 s after the pluck, relative to the strongest one at the pluck. Fading rates are illustrative.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>Which frictions keep the springs apart <span class="needs">matrices</span></summary>

A loss term $\alpha u_t + \beta A u_t$, with constants $\alpha, \beta \ge 0$, gives $q_n'' + (\alpha + \beta\lambda_n)q_n' + \lambda_nq_n = 0$: still one equation per shape, with higher shapes fading faster. A friction force $-r\,u_t(s, t)$ at one point $s$ gives instead $q_n'' + \sum_m C_{nm}q_m' + \lambda_nq_n = 0$ with $C_{nm} \propto X_n(s)X_m(s)$, a rank-one matrix that couples the shapes. Shapes with $X_n(s) = 0$ have a zero row and column in $C$, so they ring on untouched; for a light touch, each other shape drains at a rate proportional to $X_n(s)^2$.

</details>
:::

## What it took {#conditions}

Every step used one of six properties of this string; the instruments in [post 4](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd) keep some and break others.

| The string is… | Without it… |
|:--|:--|
| finite | an infinite string has no eigenfunctions with finite $\int X^2$; the sum over $n$ becomes an integral |
| tied so that $A$ is symmetric | a bridge that absorbs energy, or sound carried off into the air, makes the shapes complex and no longer perpendicular |
| tied so that $A$ is positive | ends sliding on rings let the whole string drift ($\lambda = 0$) |
| without friction, or with friction the sines split | friction at one point couples the shapes (the light touch) |
| linear: small slopes | a hard pluck raises the tension, so the pitch starts high and glides down[^jos] |
| unchanging in time | turning a peg while it rings makes each $\lambda_n$ glide; a sliding finger moves the shapes themselves |

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Reader question</span>Why eigenfunctions in $x$, and not in $t$?</summary>

Space has two edges, where a condition holds for all time; time has one start. The operator $A$ is built from the $x$-derivatives and the two edges, so its eigenfunctions are functions of $x$, and time is handled by one spring equation per shape with its two starting values. Nothing in the problem gives time a second edge. In space and time together, a product $X(x)\cos(\omega t)$ solves the equation exactly when $AX = \omega^2X$; for $X = \sin kx$ that is $\omega^2 = c^2k^2$, and the ends pick $k = n\pi/L$.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Reader question</span>Isn't every function of $(x, t)$ a sum of products $f(x)g(t)$?</summary>

Yes: products of a basis in $x$ and a basis in $t$ form a basis for functions of $(x, t)$, solution or not. (M. Reed and B. Simon, [*Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics I: Functional Analysis*](https://shop.elsevier.com/books/i-functional-analysis/reed/978-0-12-585050-6), revised ed., Academic Press, 1980, section II.4) So "a sum of products" is not what makes the method work. What makes it work is that, in the eigenbasis, each coefficient $q_n(t)$ obeys its own spring equation, so it is $a_n\cos 2\pi f_nt + b_n\sin 2\pi f_nt$, fixed by the start.

</details>
:::
